segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we were learning how we can use the present to talk about the past using haber,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: which is "to have" in sentences like: I have gone, I have eaten.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What do you think terminar means? Terminar.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: To terminate.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And what what verb would we use more commonly in English?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Finish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Finish. Terminar is to finish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Do you remember how to say I have from haber?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We can look at the two vowels we have in haber and this will set us off.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ah, yes.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Okay. So, I have?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Is it he or ha?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: It's he. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, we have?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hemos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. How do you spell he?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: H-E.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: H-E, good. And that H comes from haber, that silent H that you have there. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say, I have finished? Firstly, how do you make finished? How do you get the word finished from terminar?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So you have all the information, now you can build the sentence. I have finished.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: He terminado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. He terminado. And I finished it? I've finished it?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: He lo terminado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What is the rule about where this lo, la, me, te can go?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: It's in the beginning of the sentence actually, isn't it?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: This would be a simplification of the rule that you might find unhelpful.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Well, if it was in the to form, it would be at the end.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So after the to form, or...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Or before everything everything else?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Before the changed verb.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So this is the way we want to think about it. If we simplify the thought to 'at the beginning or at the end',

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: when there's other words there, we might be really confused about where we can put it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we must think: after the complete verb (the to form), or before the changed verb.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So if you say he lo terminado, you've actually got it after a changed verb, you've got it after he.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So this is a very rare situation in Spanish where we have two changed verbs together:

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: he terminado. We see, usually after a changed verb, we get a complete verb: quiero terminar, I want to finish;

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: puedo terminar, I can to finish;

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: debo terminar, I must, I owe to finish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So here we have two changed verbs together: he terminado. Weird situation, which means there's only one place it can go.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Before the he?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: It's lo he terminado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Lo he terminado. And I finished them?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Los he terminado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Los he terminado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So with -ar verbs, we take off the -ar and we put -ado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: With -er/-ir verbs, we take away the -er or the -ir and we put -ido to get this form of the verb that we need after haber.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Whether it's an e- there's no -edo?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Nope. Like I said, there's only one difference between -er and -ir verbs

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: in all of the Spanish language. Only one occasion where they're doing things differently and that was in the present for 'we'.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So for example we have vender, which means to sell, and how do you say we sell?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Vendemos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And we had venir, to come, and how do you say we come?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Venimos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Venimos. So we had -emos and -imos. This is the only time in the whole Spanish language that these two verbs are doing something differently.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: To get this form of the verb that we need after haber, everything goes to -ido. So vender becomes...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Vendido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Vendido. And venir becomes...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Venido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Venido. Now we understand where is bienvenido from, 'welcome'. Perder, which was to lose, becomes...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Perdido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Perdido. Good. Now we can make some sentences. How do you say I have lost?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: He perdido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: He perdido. What if you wanted to be emphatic and use the word for I to to emphasize?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Yo he perdido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Yo he perdido. And we said that there was a connection between I and we, that we is the plural of I.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So this can help us remember that there is a little connection between he for I have and we have, which is...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hemos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hemos. They both use e. He, hemos. Good. So how do you say we have lost?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hemos perdido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hemos perdido. Nosotros... nosotros is the word for we, for a male or mixed group.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: If you are just females, what do you think you might say?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Nosotras.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Nosotras. Good. You pronounced an S there, which was very good. Most English speakers find themselves accidentally saying nozotros with a Z,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: not nozotros, but nosotros, it's an S. Nosotros or nosotras. So how would you say we have lost, emphasizing?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Nosotras, sorry, nos... well, nosotros, yeah, hemos perdido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Nosotros, or nosotras if we're all females, hemos perdido. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we had he and hemos, and then for the rest of the versions we go to the other vowel which was in this word haber.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So give me the other versions. Firstly, he, she, it, you formal have, has...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ha?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So let's start with that one. How would you say he has lost?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ha perdido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And if you wanted to clarify or emphasize that it was he and not she, for example?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Il... él.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Close. Él. Good.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Él ha perdido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Él ha perdido. And she?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: La?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So you must differentiate between she and her. Don't just let that feminine idea come in your mind and pick one of these. You must take the time to decide which one is it. Is it she or is it her?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ella.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So she has lost?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ella ha perdido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. You have lost, informally?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Has perdido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Now, if you want to emphasize, if you want to say YOU have lost, the word for you for informal is tú. T-U. Tú.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tú has perdido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Tú has perdido. What was I love you?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Te quiero.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Te quiero. So what is the difference between tú and te?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: It's the same as the difference between she and her, and he and him. Only in English, we don't have two separate words for you and you in those two different positions.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: He sees, I see him.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So he sees, we use he, then I see him, we use him.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: This is very intuitive to us in English, we don't think about it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: She sees, I see her.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: There we have the same change. But you, it doesn't change:

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: you see, I see you.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So that might confuse us in Spanish because in English it doesn't change. But all we need to understand is that tú

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: goes in the group of él, ella, yo, tú (you),

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: and te is in the group of those little words: lo, la, me, te.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So let's practice this. What was to see or to view?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ver?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ver. And I see is a little bit irregular. Do you remember how it was?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Veo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say I see it, I see him, or I see you (formal)?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Lo veo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Lo veo. Good. I see her, or I see it (feminine thing), or I see you speaking formally to a female?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: La veo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: La veo. Or how would you say I see them (females), or I see you (plural, all females), or I see them (feminine objects)?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Las veo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And what if they were masculine or mixed objects or people?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Los veo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. One set of words we have me for me, we have te for you informal, we have lo for he, for masculine object, you formal, or even for neuter, which kind of just means when something doesn't have gender.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Maybe you'd say, you know, I want to see it, and that 'it' refers to a situation or something like this, you will use lo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And then from this, the other ones come, but building from lo. So you change the O to A to make it feminine, and you add your S for plural, ah?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Which means one sound is left in this little set which is us. Do you remember how is us?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Nos?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Nos. Good. So this is one set.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now let's practice the other set. How do you say he sees?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Is it ve?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And what if you want to clarify or emphasize?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Él ve.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Él ve. Good. She sees?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ella ve.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ella ve. Good. I see?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Yo veo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Now we said the word for we is nosotros, not us; us is nos. We is nosotros.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, we see?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Nosotros vemos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Nosotros vemos. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We said that you informal was tú. Tú. The you in you see: tú ves.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Which means that we have also the formal you to learn, which is usted. Usted.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Usted.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Usted. Which is the formal you. It's actually a contraction of vuestra merced, which means your honour, something like this, contracted to usted. So this is the formal you.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say you see, talking formally?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Usted ve.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. You see it, talking formally?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Lo ve usted?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Or usted lo ve. It can be either way. The word order in Spanish is much more flexible than in English. Lo ve usted, usted lo ve, either way.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say you see them, still talking formally?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Usted ve los... sorry, los ve.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Usted los ve. Good, so usted is flexible, los is not flexible, ah? Usted los ve, los ve usted.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now the word for they, the word for they is ellos. E-L-L-O-S.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And this LL in most Spanish dialects makes a 'y' sound.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You might hear ellos around Río de la Plata, in Buenos Aires, of Argentina, Montevideo in Uruguay;

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: you might hear like a 'j' kind of sound in Colombia, ellos;

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: but in the great majority of Spanish-speaking world, double L and Y make 'y'. Ellos or ellas.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I'm sure you can work out the difference between the two. What's the difference between ellos and ellas?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ellos is for males or a mixed group, and ellas is for females.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So how would you say they see, emphasizing or clarifying that it's they?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ellos... is it ven?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes. Ellos ven.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: They see them?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ellos los ven.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ellos los ven. Good. Or we could have had any combination of gender: ellas los ven, ellas las ven, ellos las ven, etc.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say they see me?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ellos me ven.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Ellos me ven. So we're understanding that we have two separate groups of very important words:

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: the set of yo, él, ella, ellos, ellas, nosotros, tú, and usted. Yo veo, tú ves, usted/él/ella ve, ellos/ellas ven, and nosotros vemos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Then we have the other set of words: me, lo, la, los, las, nos, te.
